title: Complementation and Gene Function: From Beadle and Tatum to Benzer

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A recessive allele shows its effect only when {{c1::no working allele}} is present.
cards.quote: shows its effect only when no working allele is present, so a diploid is mutant only when both copies are defective

cards.front: Why is an inactivating (loss-of-function) mutation usually recessive?
cards.back: One working copy makes enough product, so a heterozygote still has a wild-type phenotype.
cards.quote: An inactivating mutation is usually recessive because one working copy makes enough product.

cards.front: What is a compound heterozygote?
cards.back: A diploid carrying two different mutant alleles of one gene. It is mutant if both alleles are defective.
cards.quote: homozygous for one mutant allele, or a compound heterozygote carrying two different mutant alleles of one gene

cards.front: A gene's place on a chromosome is its {{c1::locus}}.
cards.quote: A gene's place on a chromosome is its locus; linkage and mapping and three-point mapping locate loci.

cards.front: In a rescue-based analysis of mutants, what can rescue not tell you about a defect?
cards.back: It narrows where the defect lies, but does not name the broken reaction or map a chromosome position.
cards.quote: Rescue narrows where a defect lies; it does not name the broken reaction or map a chromosome position.

cards.front: For recessive mutations in two different genes a and b, what is the genotype and phenotype of the trans diploid in a complementation test?
cards.back: a/+ ; b/+ (for linked genes, a + / + b). It is wild type: the mutations complement.
cards.quote: the trans diploid is a/+ ; b/+ (for linked genes, a + / + b). It is wild type: the mutations complement.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: Two recessive alleles of the same gene are combined in trans as a1/a2. Why is the diploid still mutant?
cards.back: Neither chromosome carries a working copy of the gene, so the mutations fail to complement.
cards.quote: Two alleles of one gene give a1/a2, with no working copy, so the diploid stays mutant.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: Mutations that fail to complement form a {{c1::complementation group}}, which usually marks one gene.
cards.quote: Mutations that fail to complement form a complementation group, which usually marks one gene.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: In a complementation analysis, mutant 1 fails to complement mutant 3, and mutant 3 fails to complement mutant 5. Mutant 1 complements mutant 5. Can the three form one clean complementation group under the simple model?
cards.back: No. In a simple group every pair inside it should fail to complement. Recheck the crosses and recessiveness before invoking an exception.
cards.quote: In a simple complementation group, every inside pair should fail.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: Five recessive, autosomal white-eyed fly mutants (1 to 5) are crossed in all pairs. The only crosses with white F1 are 1x3, 1x5, 3x5 and 2x4. How many complementation groups are there, and what are they?
cards.back: Two groups: {1, 3, 5} and {2, 4}. Mutants in a group fail with each other and complement the rest, so at least two genes.
cards.quote: Three complementation groups, so at least three genes.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: A complementation screen of white-eyed fly mutants finds three groups. Why does it show "at least" three genes and not exactly three?
cards.back: Other genes needed for red pigment may not have been hit by any of the mutants in the screen.
cards.quote: other genes needed for red pigment may not have been hit in these six mutants
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: Why can a complementation test not assign a dominant mutation to a gene?
cards.back: A dominant allele stays mutant opposite any partner, so its trans result is uninformative.
cards.quote: A dominant allele stays mutant opposite any partner, so its trans result is uninformative
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: How can a dominant-negative mutation mislead a complementation test?
cards.back: Its product spoils the wild-type product, so the trans diploid is mutant and the pair can falsely look like the same gene.
cards.quote: a dominant-negative product that spoils the wild-type product can falsely look like "same gene."
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: What is intragenic complementation, and in what kind of protein can it occur?
cards.back: Two differently damaged alleles of one gene can sometimes restore function. It can occur in a protein built from several identical subunits, where damaged subunits can sometimes rebuild a working enzyme.
cards.quote: In a protein built from several identical subunits, differently damaged subunits can sometimes rebuild a working enzyme: intragenic complementation.
cards.section: The complementation test: put two mutations in one cell

cards.front: Two white-eyed fly strains are crossed, and the F1 flies have red eyes. Assume each mutation is recessive and autosomal. What does this indicate?
cards.back: The strains have lost different genes, so each supplies what the other lacks. Red eye needs many genes, so different defects can give the same white phenotype.
cards.quote: Two white-eyed strains may therefore have lost different genes.
cards.section: Why white eyes can have different causes

cards.front: Why was Neurospora's haploid growing phase an advantage for finding mutants?
cards.back: With one chromosome copy, a recessive mutation shows at once, with no second working allele to hide it.
cards.quote: Its growing phase is haploid, with one chromosome copy, so a recessive mutation shows at once.
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: Why did Beadle and Tatum irradiate Neurospora fruiting bodies before meiosis?
cards.back: Each spore taken was then haploid, so a recessive mutation in it would show in its culture.
cards.quote: Beadle and Tatum irradiated fruiting bodies before meiosis, so each spore taken was haploid.
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: Outline the Beadle and Tatum screen in Neurospora, from irradiation to the mutants they kept.
cards.back: X-ray, grow single-spore cultures on complete medium, test each on minimal medium, and keep those that grow on complete but not minimal. Then add supplements one at a time to minimal medium.
cards.quote: Keep the ones that grow on complete medium but not on minimal.
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: In a Neurospora mutant that cannot grow on minimal medium, what does the single supplement that restores growth tell you?
cards.back: It names the synthesis that was lost: the mutant cannot make that compound.
cards.quote: The single compound that restores growth names the synthesis that was lost.
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: A single supplement restores growth of a Neurospora mutant. Why must the mutant still be crossed to wild type before the defect is called a single-gene mutation?
cards.back: Rescue shows a missing synthesis, not its genetic basis. The cross tests whether the inherited difference segregates as one gene.
cards.quote: Growth rescue identifies a missing synthesis, not its genetic basis.
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: What did Beadle and Tatum's 1941 Neurospora screen find among about 2,000 strains?
cards.back: Three mutants, needing pyridoxine (vitamin B6), the thiazole half of thiamine, or para-aminobenzoic acid.
cards.quote: Their 1941 paper reported three mutants among about 2,000 strains
cards.section: Beadle and Tatum: one mutant, one blocked step

cards.front: Garrod noted that alkaptonuria often appeared in children of cousins. What inheritance pattern does that suggest, and why?
cards.back: A recessive Mendelian trait, the pattern expected when it often appears in children of cousins.
cards.quote: He noted that it often appeared in children of parents who were cousins, the pattern expected for a recessive Mendelian trait
cards.section: Before the Neurospora screen

cards.front: How would you restate "one gene, one enzyme" today?
cards.back: A gene encodes a polypeptide or a functional RNA.
cards.quote: Today you would say that a gene encodes a polypeptide or a functional RNA.
cards.section: From one gene, one enzyme to gene products

cards.front: Give three reasons "one gene, one enzyme" is too simple.
cards.back: Some genes encode only RNA; alternative splicing gives one gene several proteins; an enzyme with several different subunits needs several genes.
cards.quote: Some genes encode only RNA, alternative splicing gives one gene several proteins, and an enzyme with several different subunits needs several genes.
cards.section: From one gene, one enzyme to gene products

cards.front: In growth-rescue data on mutants of one biosynthetic pathway, how do you recognize the end product?
cards.back: It rescues every mutant class, since every block lies before it.
cards.quote: Arginine rescues every class, so it is the end product.
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: What assumptions does pathway ordering from rescue data make?
cards.back: One linear route, and supplied compounds enter the cell and can be used. Each mutant has one block.
cards.quote: pathway rescue assumes one linear route whose supplied compounds enter the cell and can be used

cards.front: In a single linear pathway, compound P rescues only one mutant class, and compound Q rescues that class and a second. Which compound is earlier in the pathway?
cards.back: P. A compound rescues only mutants blocked before it, so the compound rescuing fewer classes lies earlier, as ornithine, rescuing only class A, precedes citrulline.
cards.quote: Ornithine rescues only A, so ornithine comes earlier than citrulline.
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: In the arginine pathway (precursor, ornithine, citrulline, arginine), a mutant is blocked between ornithine and citrulline. Which compound does it tend to accumulate, and on which supplements does it grow?
cards.back: Ornithine tends to build up, since its conversion is blocked. It grows on citrulline or arginine, not ornithine. A block often makes the compound just before it build up.
cards.quote: A block often makes the compound just before it build up.
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: Class C Neurospora mutants are blocked between citrulline and arginine. Why can rescue data alone not say which compound they accumulate?
cards.back: That stretch holds two reactions, so C may build up citrulline or argininosuccinate. Feedback also changes how much builds up, so accumulation has to be measured.
cards.quote: so C may build up citrulline or argininosuccinate. Rescue data alone cannot say which
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: Fifteen arginine-requiring Neurospora strains fall into only three rescue classes, yet at least seven are genetically different. What does this show about rescue classes, and what separated the genes?
cards.back: One rescue class need not be one gene: several genes can act within the same bracketed stretch. Heterokaryon tests and crosses separated the genes.
cards.quote: one rescue class need not be one gene
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: In the arginine pathway, a double mutant is blocked before ornithine and between citrulline and arginine. On which supplement will it grow, and why?
cards.back: Arginine only. A supplement must enter after every remaining block, so the block nearer arginine sets the requirement.
cards.quote: In double mutants, the block nearer arginine set the requirement, because a supplement must enter after every remaining block.
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: In Neurospora, how does a mutant blocked before ornithine respond to ornithine, citrulline and arginine?
cards.back: It grows on all three, since every supplement lies after its block. Class A in the lesson is blocked before ornithine.
cards.quote: A is blocked before ornithine, B between ornithine and citrulline, and C between citrulline and arginine.
cards.section: Ordering a pathway from rescue data

cards.front: What question does a complementation test ask, and what question does a recombination test ask?
cards.back: Complementation asks whether two mutations damage the same function. Recombination asks whether the two sites can be separated by crossing over.
cards.quote: A complementation test asks whether two mutations damage the same function. A recombination test asks whether the two sites can be separated by crossing over.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: How do phage T4 rII mutants behave on E. coli strain B and on E. coli K12S(lambda)?
cards.back: They form large plaques on B but cannot grow on K12S(lambda), a K-12 strain that carries phage lambda.
cards.quote: rII mutants form large plaques on E. coli strain B but cannot grow on K12S(λ), a K-12 strain that carries the phage lambda.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: Two T4 rII mutants coinfect K12S(lambda) and the cells release progeny. What does this show about the mutations, and why?
cards.back: They lie in different functional units: each phage supplies what the other lacks, so the mutations complement.
cards.quote: If they lie in different functional units, each phage supplies what the other lacks and the cells release progeny.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: Benzer called a unit defined by the cis-trans test a {{c1::cistron}}.
cards.quote: he called such a unit, defined by the cis-trans test, a cistron
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: Two T4 rII mutants fail to complement, yet crossing them gives wild-type recombinants. Do the results contradict each other?
cards.back: No. Failure places the mutations in one functional unit; wild-type recombinants show separable sites inside it.
cards.quote: Failure places the mutations in one functional unit; wild-type recombinants show separable sites inside it.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: In Benzer's recombination test, why are progeny plated on both E. coli B and K12S(lambda)?
cards.back: B counts all progeny, since all types grow there. K12S(lambda) counts only wild-type recombinants.
cards.quote: plate the progeny on B to count everything and on K12S(λ) to count only wild-type recombinants.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: recombination frequency = {{c1::2 × (wild-type recombinants per mL) / (total progeny per mL)}}
cards.quote: recombination frequency = 2 × (wild-type recombinants per mL) / (total progeny per mL)
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: Why is the wild-type fraction doubled in the rII recombination-frequency formula?
cards.back: The selective plate sees only wild type. The reciprocal double-mutant class is equally frequent but unseen, so it adds the same fraction again.
cards.quote: The selective plate sees one of the two reciprocal classes, so an equally recovered, unseen double-mutant class contributes the same fraction again.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: Two noncomplementing rII mutants are crossed on E. coli B. Progeny diluted 10^-5 give 120 plaques per 0.1 mL on B. Progeny diluted 10^-2 give 30 plaques per 0.1 mL on K12S(lambda). Neither parent alone grows on K12S(lambda). Assume equal reciprocal recombinant classes. What is the recombination frequency?
cards.back: 0.05 percent. Wild type: 30 x 10 x 10^2 = 3 x 10^4 per mL. Total: 120 x 10 x 10^5 = 1.2 x 10^8 per mL. Fraction 2.5 x 10^-4, doubled to 5 x 10^-4.
cards.quote: Wild-type recombinants: 40 plaques in 0.1 mL is 400 per mL; correcting for the 10^-3 dilution, 400 × 10^3 = 4 × 10^5 per mL.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A finite rII cross yields no recombinant plaques. Does that prove the two mutations occupy the identical site?
cards.back: No. The sites may be so close that the sample missed the rare recombinants. Zero recombinants set only an upper limit on separation.
cards.quote: Zero recombinants set only an upper limit on their separation; they do not prove zero distance.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure

cards.front: In an rII complementation test, mutants rX and rY fail to grow together on K12S(lambda). The double mutant rX rY plus wild type does grow. What does the control rule out?
cards.back: Dominance. The double mutant with wild type grows, so it does not interfere with wild type, and the trans failure reflects shared function.
cards.quote: the double mutant with wild type grows, so it does not interfere with wild type
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mutants rX and rY fail to complement but recombine. A third rII mutant, rZ, complements both. What can you conclude about rZ, and about the rII region?
cards.back: rZ lies in a different functional unit from rX and rY, so rII holds more than one cistron. Complementation sorts function; recombination shows separable sites within a cistron.
cards.quote: Benzer's 1955 paper found that this test split the rII region into two independent segments.
cards.section: Benzer: function versus fine structure
